augustinian_missions.title: Augustinian Missions and the Visita of Catuguian
augustinian_missions.description: Augustinian missionaries set up a mission in Gapan in 1595, which led to a Cabanatuan visita in 1750. Cabanatuan became a cabecera in 1780, and in 1846 Catuguian, then a barrio of Cabanatuan, became a visita of its mission.

nueva_ecija_provincehood.title: Nueva Ecija Becomes a Province
nueva_ecija_provincehood.description: Nueva Ecija was organized as a district (corregimiento) in 1801 and became an independent, regular province in 1848. Catuguian's population grew afterwards.

founding_of_the_pueblo.title: Catuguian Becomes an Independent Pueblo
founding_of_the_pueblo.description: Catuguian residents petitioned the alcalde-mayor of Nueva Ecija for a town. It was granted on December 11, 1852, with Catuguian as cabecera. The first barrios were La Torre, Santo Domingo (Pulong Buli), Baloc, Concepcion and Valle.

renaming_to_talavera.title: Catuguian Renamed Talavera
renaming_to_talavera.description: A petition filed on February 4 asked to rename the town after Talavera de la Reina in Spain. It was approved on February 14. Some versions say February 11 or 14, so the exact day needs verification.

spanish_era_development.title: Education, Growth and Parish Recognition
spanish_era_development.description: A royal decree of 20 December 1863 established separate primary schools for boys and girls in each pueblo. By 1866 the population was 4,421. On November 20, 1872, a Royal Decree by King Amadeo I recognized the Parroquia de Talavera as an independent parish. Extensive grasslands also made Talavera a major cattle supplier for Manila.

philippine_american_war.title: Occupation by General Lawton
philippine_american_war.description: During the Philippine-American War, Talavera was occupied by American General Henry Lawton. The source gives no exact year.

boundary_changes_american_period.title: Territorial Adjustments
boundary_changes_american_period.description: Sitio Bacal was annexed in 1910 (Executive Order No. 39, s. 1909). Eight sitios were separated in 1912 to form Muñoz (EO No. 72). Barrio Lomboy was annexed in 1914 (EO No. 25). Barrio San Francisco went to Santo Domingo in 1937 (EO No. 96).

landlordism_and_peasant_struggles.title: Haciendas and Tenancy Conflicts
landlordism_and_peasant_struggles.description: Migration increased as haciendas and cattle grazing expanded. Peasant struggles over landlordism and shared tenancy appeared in San Ricardo, Bantug, Casili and Morcon.

japanese_occupation_and_hukbalahap.title: Japanese Occupation and Birth of Squadron 8
japanese_occupation_and_hukbalahap.description: The Imperial Japanese Army occupied Talavera in December 1941. Hukbalahap Squadron 8 was formed in Talavera with more than 100 members.

liberation_and_pow_rescue.title: Defense Line and Rescue of 510 Prisoners
liberation_and_pow_rescue.description: San Pascual and Pinagpanaan became a strategic defense line against the retreating Japanese army. Barangay Sibul served as a rendezvous point for 510 rescued prisoners of war from Camp Pangatian.

huklandia.title: Post-War Huk Expansion
huklandia.description: After the war, Huk forces expanded in Nueva Ecija, in what was known as 'Huklandia'. Talavera was part of this area.

creation_of_llanera.title: Barrios Annexed to Llanera
creation_of_llanera.description: General Luna, Morcon, Mabini, Ricarte, Casili and Picon, along with Plaridel and Bosque, were annexed to the new municipality of Llanera under Republic Act 1221.

local_history_book.title: Ang Kasaysayan ng Talavera
local_history_book.description: Mayor Romeo F. Maliwat commissioned public librarian Tomas I. Pagaduan to compile Talavera's history. It was published in 1967 and is likely the best local primary source.

munoz_boundary_dispute.title: Bakal and Matingkis Dispute with Muñoz
munoz_boundary_dispute.description: The Science City of Muñoz claimed barangays Bakal I, II, III and Matingkis. Talavera's Sangguniang Bayan rejected the claims in October 1998. The claims were set aside in March 1999, confirming Talavera's jurisdiction.

heritage_recognition.title: Cultural Properties Declared
heritage_recognition.description: The Gabaldon Building was recognized as built heritage in February 2019. Sicsican Bridge and the Tal-Acacia Tree were declared cultural properties in 2020.

cityhood_proposal.title: Bills to Convert Talavera into a Component City
cityhood_proposal.description: Rep. Estrellita Suansing filed a House bill in July 2019, and a Senate bill followed in February 2021. Wikipedia's text says House Bill 184 but its reference says 194, so check the number.

population_2024.title: 2024 Census
population_2024.description: The 2024 Census of Population counted 137,444 residents, declared official in July 2025.

facts.title: The Vegetable Basket of Nueva Ecija
facts.description: Talavera's nickname reflects its farming economy. Older versions of the Wikipedia article also call it the "Milk Capital" and the "Food basket in Inland Luzon".

facts.title: Named After a Spanish City
facts.description: In 1853, Catuguian was renamed Talavera after Talavera de la Reina in Spain.

facts.title: From 4,421 to 137,444
facts.description: Talavera had 4,421 inhabitants in 1866 and 137,444 in the 2024 census.

facts.title: 53 Barangays
facts.description: Talavera is divided into 53 barangays. Some are exclaves surrounded by the Science City of Muñoz.

facts.title: Manila's Cattle Supplier
facts.description: Under Spanish rule, Talavera's extensive grasslands made it a major cattle supplier for the Manila market.

facts.title: Gatas ng Kalabaw Festival
facts.description: Celebrated every May 12 to 15, it promotes carabao's milk and culminates in the town fiesta for St. Isidore the Worker.
